I’M SURPRISED I was never fired. For more than 20 years as a personal trainer, new clients often hired me to help them lose belly fat. They’d been led to believe abdominal crunches were the solution. Crunch, crunch, crunch! Very rarely did I have my clients do crunches.
The science was on my side. In a 2011 study, adults did seven abdominal exercises, five days a week, for six weeks. Their ab muscles got stronger. Their stubborn belly fat didn’t budge. You can’t crunch your way to a flat stomach. Fat comes off only by adhering to a thorough program, including how you eat, how you move, how hard you train and how well you sleep.
So what did we do instead? We built the core. Not the visible six-pack muscle on the surface, but the deep layers that wrap around your trunk like a corset. Their main job isn’t to curl you forward. It’s to hold you steady while your arms and legs do the work. Every heavy grocery bag or suitcase lift, every hike or bike ride, every grandchild you scoop off the floor runs through your core.
When the core is weak, injuries follow. Researchers tracked 277 college athletes for three years. For the women, poor control of the trunk predicted ligament and ACL injuries in the knee with roughly 90% accuracy. A weak core showed up as a hurt knee.
The military figured this out, too. The Army and the Navy have both dropped sit-ups from their fitness tests. The plank took their place.
Now I’m a financial planner. And I risk getting fired all over again.
Financial Crunches
Today’s clients don’t seek to reduce their belly fat. They seek returns. Should I buy the stock everyone’s talking about? Should I get out before the next drop? Which fund is outperforming?
These are financial crunches. They feel productive. You’re actively doing lots of buying, selling, trading. But focusing on returns can often slow your progress toward your goals.
Sometimes the wrong reps even move you backward. Morningstar found that over the 10 years through 2024, the average dollar invested in U.S. funds earned about 7% a year. The funds themselves earned 8.2%. The gap came mostly from investors buying and selling at the wrong times.
Your wealth, like your waistline, responds best to a comprehensive program. It isn’t flashy. But it’s what works.
Your Financial Core
Your financial core is the ongoing work that, over time, holds everything steady:
A savings rate that rises with your income.
An emergency fund for when life throws you a curveball.
Insurance that matches the risks you actually face.
Tax planning that determines which accounts you fund and which you draw from first.
An estate plan built for your legacy wishes.

Investments are the arms and legs. They create the movement. Without a strong core, the power leaks out and the risk of a financial injury increases. A market drop with no cash reserve forces you to sell low. A disability with no coverage drains years of savings. That’s the financial version of a blown knee.
How Hard Should You Work?
In my last article, I asked what financial RPE you should strive for. In fitness, RPE represents rate of perceived exertion. With money, I think of RPE as your rate of perceived EFFORT. On a scale of one to 10, how hard are you working toward your goals?
The answer changes as you age. Here’s how I coach my clients:
Your 20s: Aim for a 5. Have fun. Ease into all things adult. Spend less than you earn, capture your full employer match and start a Roth. Build a strong social life and keep learning. Friends, family and skills compound, too. They’ll serve you well in every decade that follows.
Your 30s: Aim for a 7. This is progressive overload. You’ve built some strength, so it’s time to add weight. Your income grows, and so does what you’re carrying: a partner, a mortgage, maybe little ones. Let your savings grow right along with your paycheck. When other people start depending on you or your income, do what it takes to make sure they’d be okay without you. Life insurance gets your attention before college savings.
Your 40s: Aim for a 9. Peak earning years collide with growing kids, aging parents and the busiest calendar of your life. This isn’t the 9 I warned about last time, where people grind so hard they miss their children growing up. This 9 comes from the load life puts on you. At times it will feel like running uphill on a treadmill when someone else keeps increasing the speed and incline. Simply staying on track takes real effort.
Push retirement savings toward the max and keep your focus on the goals you’re trying to achieve. If you are raising children, you will likely be shocked at how much money is being spent and lifestyle creep may arise in the form of paying for convenience. This is when retirement and tax planning get serious.
Your 50s: Aim for an 8. Think of the final weeks before a marathon. The hardest training runs are behind you. Race day is approaching so you start picturing crossing that finish line. When will you stop working? What will a typical week look like? Where will your paycheck come from? How much can you spend and not risk running out of money? The choices you make now shape the next 30 years, and many are hard to undo.
Your 60s: Aim for a 7, then downshift to a 5. A little bit of effort remains before you cross the finish line. Cheers! Remember those relationships and cool things you began engaging with in your 20s? Now you have the time and hopefully the means to make the best of this next chapter. It’ll be great to have dear friends to enjoy this time with. Your lifelong habit of continuing to learn can support brain health and cognition.
Your 70s and beyond: Aim for a 4. I used to tell my personal training clients that a walk didn’t count as cardiovascular exercise unless your heart rate achieved the low end of your target heart rate zone. Think of this stage as a brisk walk. Easy enough to enjoy, but still enough effort to keep the results you worked so hard for.
If your 50s feel like an RPE of a 10 and you simply can’t sustain that level of effort, it’s usually because your effort was too low in the decades before. Keep the 20s and 30s at a steady cadence, and you’ll earn yourself the right to ease off later.
Build the Core
My training clients wanted flat stomachs. I guided them to strong cores, fewer injuries and the ability to live life with strength and confidence.
Money works the same way. Build the foundation first. Keep your effort consistent. Embrace the high-effort seasons. Enjoy the easy ones.
There comes a point where there’s no time left to play catch-up. We can’t reverse past decisions, with our health or with our money.
So skip the crunches. Train your core. And keep tabs on your financial RPE. You won’t regret it.

Annie Garland, CFP®, is a wealth advisor at WealthClarity in Lakewood, Colorado. She spent more than 20 years as a personal trainer before becoming a CFP® professional. She’s a proud mom of two daughters, a wife, and an avid mountain biker.
